en: And snatched a little sleep.
The long-limbed madman
Lay utterly unconcerned,
Esteeming the entire world
No more than the hem of his robe.
Until the seven days were complete,
Until the appointed word came due,
Until the time arrived,
The long-limbed madman
Sank into a giant’s sleep.
His true snores split the rocks;
For six days he slept,
Lying on his side at ease,
His soul steeped in restful comfort.
When he had slept his fill,
He led the rested Tookyzyl
To graze on fresh grass
And quenched its thirst
At a cold, clear spring.
Leading it about for a long while,
He filled the handsome charger’s
Broad chest with grass;
Then, leading it a little farther,
He filled the swinging-jawed stallion’s
Bare belly with grass.
Wondering whether they would come to wrestle,
And fearing brave Seytek,
He saddled Tookyzyl.
Fearing for his precious life,
He adjusted and donned his arrow-proof armor;
His destructive nature was plain.
Sarybai, son of the ogre—
Such was the extent of his courage.
His thoughts wandered in doubt,
And his ordeal took on another aspect:
“All I have found and gathered—
Perhaps I shall leave it scattered behind.
Perhaps I should somehow outwit that slave
And make my escape.
But rather than flee until I die,
I will die in battle.
Alas, Seytek is a true hero,
A lion surpassing all other youths.
This formidable Seytek
Is the head of the mighty Kyrgyz.
His courage is abundant and his wrath is fierce;
He is the black foundation stone of a dungeon.
When his ribs are fully hardened,
When the flesh fills out upon his shanks,
When the time of his maturity comes,
Will any mortal dare face him?
Will any mortal advance against him?
When his marrow is filled with milk,
When his bones mature and his strength is full,
Will any mortal dare face him?
Will any man who confronts him survive?
Will one who comes to grapple with him
Not die before his destined hour?
His massive strength is like a mountain.
This formidable youth’s
People are a forest and fortress around him.
His conflict is a terrible wrath;
When he charges, he is a lion,
A red-glowing ember—
There is none like him among mankind.
His bearing and bodily strength
Are like a taut bow of dark hardwood.
When his savage fury falls upon a man,
He smashes even stone to powder
And sweeps everything utterly away.
How exceedingly sharp his sword is!
Such is its cutting edge.
Once his spear strikes, it does not release;
Such is the hero’s courage.
It could tear and stretch the corners of a mouth.
The youth’s keen force
Is like the steel bullet of a mighty gun,
His wrath like flame—
Such is his boundless courage.
When the youth thrusts with his spear,
The ribs crack apart,
The hero’s heart gives a start,
And he shatters the spine in ten places.
The devastating youth
Seems utterly beyond measure.
Ever since I became Sarybai,
Ever since I mounted a steed bearing that name,
Ever since I put on the golden crown,
Ever since I ascended the golden throne
And ruled the people and governed the realm,
Living under the name of Sarybai,
How many times
Have I witnessed ruinous, mighty battles
While roaming the earth?
Yet fate never overtook me, and I did not die.
Never have I seen so great an ordeal in battle,
Never have I suffered such humiliation.
Clashing with this wrathful foe,
This blood-spilling raven of a boy,
Contending with this relentless youth,
The face of my right shoulder aches,
The edge of my spine aches,
The breastbone beneath my white armor aches,
And my precious heart itself aches.
Has the spear wounded it,
So that my heart rolls over?
Has it leapt out of its sheath?
Can it be that through this raven-like boy
My appointed death has somehow come?
My hunched back itself aches,
And death’s black eye brings anguish.
The relentless youth who faced me
Has launched a furious campaign;
He has shattered everything upon me
And left it falling to pieces.”
His palate trilled as he marveled in amazement.
From the venom of the struggle,
Eyes dim, the earth shifts,
The mirage flies, the people move.
Girding his renowned waist,
When yesterday they stood face-to-face,
A fierce clash began.
My fly-like soul shrieked,
Every bone in my body throbbed,
My whole frame shuddered,
My body turned to fire,
And began to burn away.
My child was slaughtered,
Doom overtook this wretched soul;
All my mighty strength
Nearly deserted me.
Once encountered, none leaves his place;
I nearly departed.
Like the rising moon, bulging forth,
I nearly sank away.
At the hands of a mere elbow-high boy,
True death came, misery seethed,
My eyes closed and blood surged—
I nearly saw my end.
It seems that by the boy Seytek
I was nearly killed.
Both arms that gave me strength ache,
My heroic courage, my manly limbs—
All ache without moving.
One edge of my marrow aches,
My very allotted span aches,
Everything I know as mine aches.
My head throbs without relief,
As though struck by an axe’s fury;
My back aches without relief—
Has affliction entered me?
This battle is a grievous affair;
Our strength has utterly failed.
Sarybai, distressed,
Unable to stand for grief,
His heart aflame, his liver an ember—
Brave Seytek had become his match.
He had no band to bear him up,
No Chañdayak warrior’s hand
To sit beside him as his support.
This world that crushes men—
Such a burning world it is.
My fly-like soul shrieking,
I would stand there sobbing,
My spirits unable to rise.
If I fight face-to-face,
If true death comes by my hand,
My heroism has been humbled;
I was a wave, now stilled.
The moon has darkened into night;
I go toward death and doom.
Was I destined to miss death in the field,
Was this the day death would come?
If Death summons, it casts its spell, it seems;
Upon the mighty bowman
It lays its cold hand, it seems.
We walk among the living,
Created as mortal servants;
When the poor soul closes its eyes,
It is shut in the grave it sees but once—
Such is harsh, true falsehood.
From the stony ravine where battle rages,
From the barren gorge where no bird flies,
A shudder came and consciousness fled.
From the thick-ranked rocky gorge,
Fighting in this way,
Across the broad open field,
Sweetly arrayed for display,
Among a singular people who race their horses,
He was a lion born to fight.
In the deep valley of Keng-Kol,
Along the great Talas,
Sarybai was a hero—
Is it fitting to fear a child?
Could a ravenous lion be fainthearted,
Could he be a fool like me?
The Kyrgyz are those I shall fight,
The great prince Semetey.
I shall destroy the Argyn camp,
I shall destroy the Nogai stronghold,
I shall lay waste the Kyrgyz marches.
Leaving not a scrap of this people—
Could a witless coward who fears a child
Be a hero like me?
The fate ordained by the Creator
I have witnessed many times before.
Finding no mountain to strike,
Finding no enemy to fight,
Finding no stone to grind my teeth upon,
Finding no head to sever,
Driven wild by restless ardor,
Like a wolf straining at its tether,
Stirred up by the very wind—
It seems I came to suffer grievous pain
At the hands of this boy.
It seems I came to die
At the hands of lion-hearted Seytek.
Our dream has turned awry;
Our cause has been undone.
Ah, Seytek is a true hero,
His fortune is complete;
He has eighty-four weapons,
And their sweep is fire.
He is a fierce one born of the Kyrgyz;
Never has his like existed in an age.
Seytek became an ember in my heart.
My name is brave Sarybai,
The courser beneath me is my wings;
To make the whole world tremble
Has ever been my custom.
My host beyond counting is assembled;
I applied all my heroic skill,
But found no way at all.
He is a boy beyond reckoning;
I shall drive a spear into his breast.
I shall thrust the spear with force,
Smash him into fragments,
And hurl him aside in pieces.
I shall slaughter his village and take the spoils;
If the day does not end, I shall return.
An omen is evil, a dream is evil,
When fortune turns against you, the deed is evil,
And evil is the coat you lift to wear.”
Not a foal remained among the shod horses;
The uproar had wholly vanished.
I, Sarybai, bearing the name of khan—
Evil is the force that abandoned me.
Evil is the force of an outsider’s son,
Evil is strife that comes from within,
Evil is fire that rises from the core.
Chañdayak, who deserted me—
Evil is the dog who knew my secrets.
If true death comes, let me die;
Let me see what courage there is
In that sniveling boy.
